solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Igor trained on piano, a Russian speciality

parts.note: P is the music abbreviation for piano, softly

indicators.note: trained on means drilled and re-formed, so the name is rearranged

explanation.surface: A Russian man practised the piano as his specialist skill.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a pianist named Igor, but the name is only letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A pirog is a large Russian pie, a traditional national dish.

clue.text: Oxford college set up member in Strasbourg out of funds

indicators.note: in a down answer, set up means written upwards, so turned round

parts.note: a Member of the European Parliament, which sits in Strasbourg

explanation.surface: An Oxford college has set up a European politician who has run out of money.
explanation.walkthrough: MEP is Member of the European Parliament; Strasbourg is one of its seats, so the city stands in for the institution.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this is one of the constituent colleges of the University of Oxford, and Cambridge has one of the same name.

clue.text: What's left except for a souvenir?

indicators.note: everything bar the A, so the A is taken out

parts.note: the remainder is what is left over

explanation.surface: A wry question: is a souvenir all you have left after the holiday?
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the rueful joke that a souvenir is all that remains of the holiday.
explanation.definitionFit: A souvenir is kept to bring back memories of a place, which is exactly what a reminder does.

clue.text: Long story forgotten, including its twist?

parts.note: its = the, the definite article standing for the possessive

explanation.surface: A long tale is forgotten, twist ending and all.
explanation.walkthrough: WIND must be read as the verb that rhymes with find, not the breeze. Margaret Mitchell's novel runs to over a thousand pages, hence 'Long story'.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Margaret Mitchell's Civil War novel is famously long, over a thousand pages, and its film nearly four hours.

clue.text: Periodically green couple use less energy after 1/12

indicators.note: after puts the later pieces behind the date

parts.note: 1/12 is the British way of writing the first of December: DEC I

indicators.note: less means without, so the energy letter is dropped from use

parts.note: E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: An eco-tip: from the first of December a couple should cut energy use, being green from time to time.
explanation.walkthrough: In British date order 1/12 is 1 December, read as DEC + I.
explanation.definitionFit: Deciduous trees shed leaves each autumn, so they are only green for part of the year, in cycles.

clue.text: Platform helps with AI being delayed

indicators.note: with AI being delayed means that pair of letters is held back and comes later in the word

explanation.surface: A stage helps, though the artificial intelligence is late.
explanation.walkthrough: AI reads as artificial intelligence in the surface, but it is just the opening pair of letters, which slip one place back behind the D.
explanation.definitionFit: A dais is a raised stage in a hall for speakers.

clue.text: Prisoner thought the experience was hell!

parts.note: 'found it hell' = thought the experience was hell

explanation.surface: An inmate reports that his time inside was hell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hell' does double duty: it completes the prisoner's verdict (found it hell) and alone is the exclamation the answer means.
explanation.definitionFit: Both 'Hell!' and 'Confound it!' are mild oaths of annoyance.

clue.text: Getting free delighted fish in dark twisted net

indicators.note: the pieces go inside the word for dark
twisted means bent out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A happy fish caught in a dark, tangled net is getting free.
explanation.definitionFit: Disentanglement is the process of extricating oneself, becoming free of a snare or complication.

clue.text: Staff shop for booze which Charlie cracks open

parts.note: an offie is an off-licence, a British liquor store
C is Charlie in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: At the liquor store, someone named Charlie cracks open a bottle.
explanation.walkthrough: An offie is British slang for an off-licence, a shop selling alcohol to take away.
explanation.definitionFit: The office can mean the staff who work there collectively.

clue.text: Ice starts to trouble experienced brothers on the climb

indicators.note: in a down answer, climbing means reading upward
the start of each word is what is taken, here the opening letters of trouble and experienced

parts.note: first letters of trouble and experienced

explanation.surface: A mountaineering scene: ice causes early problems for climbing brothers.
explanation.walkthrough: The climbing brothers belong to the surface; the ice they meet on the mountain is the dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: A sorbet is a water ice, a frozen dessert.

clue.text: Large tasteless house from 1900 redeveloped as "old" inn

indicators.note: redeveloped means rebuilt, so the letters are reworked

explanation.surface: A vulgar mansion dates from 1900 and was converted, as an old tavern.
explanation.definitionFit: A McMansion is a large, showy, mass-built house thought to lack taste.

clue.text: Bed for homeless surfer? Right, up to a point

parts.note: a sofa-surfer sleeps on friends' sofas

explanation.surface: Someone asks where a homeless sofa-surfer sleeps, and gets a grudging 'right, up to a point'.
explanation.walkthrough: A sofa-surfer or couch-surfer is someone without a home who sleeps on friends' sofas; the question mark flags that this bed is described cryptically.
explanation.definitionFit: 'So far' means to a limited extent, up to a point, as in 'I trust him only so far'.

clue.text: Celebrity touching this minute kitten's tail

indicators.note: the last letter of kitten

explanation.surface: A celebrity touching a kitten's tail right now, as in a viral photo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Celebrity' is the abstract noun, fame, not a famous person.
explanation.definitionFit: Celebrity in its older abstract sense, the state of being famous rather than a famous person, is a plain synonym here.

clue.text: Coastal road that's lovely, with a small market

parts.note: cor! is a British exclamation of admiration
a niche market is a small specialised one

explanation.surface: A travel blurb praising a lovely coastal road with a little market along it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cor!' is a British working-class exclamation, roughly 'wow', so it can stand for 'that's lovely!'.
explanation.definitionFit: A corniche is a road cut into a cliff along a coast.

clue.text: Small planet full of holes dug for extracting slime

indicators.note: the planet is filled with the holes, so contains them

parts.note: the red planet, the outer part
mines are holes dug to extract minerals

explanation.surface: A small planet riddled with mining holes is being used to extract slime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slime' is the figurative sense, oily ingratiation, and sits at the end looking like the thing being extracted.
explanation.definitionFit: Slime, in the sense of oily flattery, is smarminess.

clue.text: Taking nut, fix IKEA lamp to cabin's exterior

indicators.note: the letters are fixed up into a new order
only the outside letters of cabin

parts.note: outer letters of cabin, added to the fodder

explanation.surface: Flat-pack instructions: take a nut and fix the IKEA lamp to the outside of the cabin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking nut' looks like an instruction from the assembly leaflet; read it as one noun phrase, a nut (crazy person) who takes things.
explanation.definitionFit: A kleptomaniac compulsively steals, so is a nut for taking things.

clue.text: Settle report of explosion you heard recently

parts.note: a pop is the sound of a small explosion

indicators.note: what is heard is a sound, so we take the letter that sounds like 'you'

explanation.surface: A news report asks whether you heard the explosion recently, and to settle the matter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Report' here is the bang itself, not a news story. 'Settle' is the verb meaning to colonise.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the colonising sense: to settle a territory is to fill it with inhabitants.

clue.text: Homeless shelters buy up military art

parts.note: a stray has no home; the outer part

indicators.note: in a down answer, up means written upwards, so turned round

explanation.surface: Homeless shelters buying up military art as an investment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Homeless shelters' reads as a noun phrase, but Homeless is the stray and shelters is the verb doing the containing.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym from the Greek strategia, generalship: the discipline of planning a war.

clue.text: Course's marker showing skill in smart job

indicators.note: one thing placed in another sits inside it

parts.note: to smart is to sting; the outer part

explanation.surface: A golf-course marker shows how skilful someone was at a smart job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smart' is the verb, to sting, not the adjective meaning clever or well dressed. The course is a racecourse.
explanation.definitionFit: The starting post marks where a race begins on a racecourse.

clue.text: Be careful with bread sons pinch into shape

parts.note: to crimp is to pinch edges into folds, as on a pie

explanation.surface: Baking advice: careful with the dough, sons, pinch it into shape.
explanation.walkthrough: Bread is slang for money, so being careful with bread is being thrifty; the surface wants it to be the loaf.
explanation.definitionFit: To scrimp is to be very economical with money.

clue.text: Sexy character's promises likely to come to nothing

definitions.text: promises likely to come to nothing

parts.note: an air is a manner or character; the 's is 'is', joining the parts

explanation.surface: A seductive charmer's promises are unlikely to be kept.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's after character is 'is', gluing the wordplay to the definition, rather than a possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: empty talk, the kind of big promise that evaporates like warm air.

clue.text: Almost right, racket shortened as mid-winter approaches?

parts.note: a din is a loud noise

explanation.surface: A near-miss racket cut short as winter comes on, like a tennis season ending.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Racket shortened' looks like a deletion instruction, but 'shortened' belongs to the definition: the days have closed in.
explanation.definitionFit: Days are said to close in, becoming shorter, as midwinter approaches.

clue.text: Petrifying woman alarmed US Airbnb hosts

indicators.note: the phrase holds the answer inside it, as a host has guests

parts.note: the letters run across the end of alarmed, all of US, and the start of Airbnb

explanation.surface: A terrifying woman scared the Americans who were hosting her through Airbnb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Petrifying' is literal: this woman turned people to stone.
explanation.definitionFit: Medusa, the Gorgon of Greek myth, turned anyone who looked at her to stone.

clue.text: Sound from butchered birds is horrible

indicators.note: what we need is how the word sounds

parts.note: fowl are birds, especially poultry for the table

explanation.surface: The noise from slaughtered birds is horrible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Butchered' tells you the birds are poultry, the kind called fowl.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the word covers anything offensive or nasty, just as horrible does.

clue.text: Two eating butter sent back fine Japanese dishes

indicators.note: something sent back goes the way it came
what eats something takes it inside

parts.note: 2 in Roman numerals; the outer part
a ram butts with its head

explanation.surface: Two diners eating butter send back their fine Japanese dishes.
explanation.walkthrough: A butter is 'one who butts', so a ram, not the dairy spread. Dishes are the porcelain itself, not food.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a Japanese porcelain named after its export port, prized for plates and bowls.

clue.text: Without any price, free of charge

parts.note: ex = without, as in ex dividend

explanation.surface: Something offered without any price is free of charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Free of charge' means without cost in the surface; as a definition it means clear of an accusation.
explanation.definitionFit: A legal sense: 'charge' is an accusation, and the verb means to clear a person of one.

clue.text: Heavenly secretary tormented sad liar

parts.note: PA, personal assistant, is a secretary

indicators.note: tormented means twisted in torment, so the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: A divine assistant torments an unhappy fibber.
explanation.definitionFit: Paradisal means like paradise, blissful and divine.

clue.text: Shirt without buttons nursery cleared out is extra small

indicators.note: the middle of nursery is emptied, leaving its ends

explanation.surface: A buttonless shirt the nursery has cleared out is in size extra small.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extra small' looks like a clothing size on the label; here it is just the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal, childlike synonym: baby talk for tiny, a fit for the nursery in the surface.
